blocks.text: Billy had seen his aunt beside the Defender editor’s telephone. He had heard her tell him to leave Daniel alone. Neither was proof that she had helped pay for a robot. Eleanor knew it, and Billy knew she knew it.

Daniel’s laboratory offered no easy answers. Its shutters were down, and Billy knew Daniel would not leave a convenient list of backers inside. He stood across from it, looking at the neighboring doors instead. Somebody owned the building. Somebody collected the rent.

The first address in an old city directory led to a locked office. A repairman at the next building remembered a different agent, but his number had been disconnected. The property record named a management company with no listing Billy could find. Two afternoons of calls left him with a full notebook and no person to question.

That evening he went to his aunt’s house. Billy had used the side gate since he was a boy; he knew which bin held the paper set out for collection. He felt foolish lifting its lid. He felt worse when he remembered the officers ordered to wait while Daniel’s machine ran.

There were old newspapers, donation requests and a stack of envelopes with nothing inside. At the bottom, he found three torn pieces of a rent notice. He fitted them together on the paving stone. The address matched Daniel’s lab. Eleanor’s name appeared beside it. The return address led to a narrow office behind a hardware shop.

blocks.alt: Inspector Billy, Eleanor Blackwell’s short stocky nephew in a brown trench coat and plaid cap, pieces together torn paper from the household trash beside the side gate of her Cleveland home at dusk.
blocks.text: Billy copied the return address into his notebook. A torn notice could point him somewhere; it could not tell him who had actually paid the rent. He slipped the scraps into an envelope and closed the bin. Then he went to find the landlord.
By the time Billy reached the little office, the man inside was closing for the day.
The landlord was broad-shouldered, with a gray beard and a face that suggested he had already been disappointed by three people that afternoon. He kept one hand on the office door.
“What do you want with Orkleson?” he asked.
“We went to school together,” Billy said.
“Good. Tell your old schoolmate the rent’s due. That Blackwell lady can afford it.”

blocks.alt: Inspector Billy, a short stocky private investigator in a plaid cap and brown trench coat, questions a gruff gray-bearded landlord outside his modest Cleveland office near Daniel Orkleson's boarded laboratory.
blocks.text: Billy kept his pencil still. “Which Blackwell lady?” The landlord squinted at him. “Silver hair. Dark glasses. Comes from that family with its name on everything. She never seemed short of money until this month.”
Billy asked whether the payments were made in her name. The landlord started to shut the door. “I don’t show my books to people off the street.”
“Fair enough,” Billy said. “But if Daniel says he paid you, a name in your book settles it. I’ll come back when you have time.” He gave the man his card and left before the door closed in his face.

The next morning, the landlord called. Daniel had not paid. He wanted the account clear before another bill went out, and he would let Billy look at the receipts if Billy told him where to find his old schoolmate. Billy could not promise that. He went anyway.

At the little office desk, he compared the address on the lease with the laboratory’s door. It matched. The tenant was Daniel Orkleson. The duplicate receipts for the last several months carried another name: Eleanor Blackwell. The landlord had written it out in full each time she paid. The most recent rent was overdue.
“That’s her?” Billy asked.
“That’s who sent the money,” the landlord said. “Usually by driver. Once she brought it herself. I remember the glasses.”

With the landlord watching, Billy made copies of the lease page and the receipts at the shop next door. The landlord signed a short statement that the copies came from his records. Billy gave him a number where he could be reached if Daniel appeared.

The papers proved Eleanor had paid for Daniel’s laboratory. They did not prove what she knew about the robot. Billy held them carefully anyway. That was farther than he had managed to get since the fight.

At the Defender, Jenny was arranging interview questions when Billy came through the newsroom. Her editor had sent her to cover Eleanor’s campaign launch. In less than an hour, she was due to speak with the prospective candidate before the public announcement at Cleveland City Hall.

Billy laid the copies on the corner of her desk, away from the other reporters. Jenny read the name, then read it again. She asked where he had found the records and whether the landlord would confirm them. Billy gave her every step, including the doors that had gone nowhere.

blocks.alt: In the 1987 Cleveland Defender newsroom, Billy quietly shows Jenny, in her civilian reporter clothes, copied laboratory rent receipts naming Eleanor Blackwell while typewriters and desks fill the background.
blocks.text: Jenny pressed the copies flat beneath her hand. “If this isn’t true, I’ll be fired. The Blackwell name means something in this city. Claude has done good work here, and I won’t drag him into a story about Eleanor without a reason.”
“The receipts name her,” Billy said. “Not him.”
“I see that. I’m asking her about it. Then I’m checking every line before a word goes to print.” She put the copies into her folder. “Did she know what Daniel was building?”
“I don’t know. But officers were told to hold back when his equipment was at the lake. If she wins the mayor’s office and she’s still protecting him, he could do whatever he likes in this city.”
Jenny looked at the empty space on her question sheet. She wrote Daniel Orkleson there, underlined it once, and went to keep her appointment.

City Hall was busy with cameras, aides and people hoping for a first look at the campaign. Eleanor received Jenny in a small room off the main hall. Her silver curls were neat; dark glasses hid her eyes. She answered questions about streets, repairs and public safety without once looking at the notes Jenny held.
“The robot damaged Superior Avenue,” Jenny said. “Daniel Orkleson built it. What would you have done when it reached the street?”
“I would have expected the police to stop it,” Eleanor said.
“They hadn’t arrived when the Defenders pulled people out of its path.”
Eleanor straightened a page that was already straight. “I’m glad no more people were hurt. But we can’t have vigilantes making their own rules for Cleveland.”
“Would that include the people who stopped Orkleson’s machine?”
Her smile tightened. “If they show up again and interfere with police work, I may have them arrested.”

Jenny felt heat rise in her face. She thought of Seth holding up the falling beam, of Fist driving Luke away, of Perch trapped behind glass. She kept her voice even. “People saw those same figures saving lives. Would you ask the police why they were held back?”
“I would ask for a full account,” Eleanor said. “From everyone involved.”
Jenny wrote that down. Then she asked the question she had brought in her folder. “Have you been paying the rent on Daniel Orkleson’s laboratory?”

For the first time, Eleanor paused. She turned one pearl earring between her fingers. “I’ve supported many kinds of work in Cleveland, Miss Jenkins. My office can review a question about an individual payment.”
“Will they answer today?” Jenny asked.
An aide opened the door. The announcement was starting. Eleanor rose. “You may send them your questions.”
Jenny had no answer, and no denial. She wrote down Eleanor’s exact words before following her into the hall.

blocks.alt: Eleanor Blackwell announces her Cleveland mayoral campaign at City Hall in 1987 while civilian reporter Jenny Jenkins takes composed notes despite anger, and Billy watches from the back of the gathering.
blocks.text: Outside Cleveland City Hall, Eleanor faced the cameras and announced that she would run for mayor. Applause rose around Jenny. Billy stood at the back of the crowd, watching his aunt promise a safer city.

Jenny closed her notebook on the promise. She would report the arrest threat, check the rent records again, and give Eleanor’s office a chance to answer. Beside the steps, Billy thought of Daniel somewhere in Cleveland, still free. If Eleanor won, the man who had built the robot might have City Hall clearing his path.
